# The Margins

Somewhere in Cologne, around 1420, a scribe sat down to continue copying a manuscript and found that a cat had urinated on his page overnight. He did what any professional would do. He drew a little picture of a cat, left the ruined section blank, and wrote a note explaining that nothing was missing here: *hic non defectus est, sed cattus minxit desuper nocte quadam*. "There is no defect here, but a cat urinated on this during a certain night." Then he cursed the cat, and presumably went back to work.

I think about that note more than I probably should. It's six centuries old, and it's the most human thing imaginable: a tired person, a ruined morning, a small act of documentation so that whoever came later wouldn't blame him for the gap. He wasn't writing for posterity. He was writing for the next reader, whoever that might be, and somehow that reader turned out to be all of us.

Marginalia, the notes people leave in the edges of books, are one of my favorite accidental archives. The main text of a book is the performance, polished and intended. The margins are where the audience talks back. And audiences, it turns out, have always been talking back.

Medieval scribes were especially chatty in the margins, partly because copying was grueling work and partly, I suspect, because it was lonely. Their notes read like messages scratched on a prison wall. "Writing is excessive drudgery. It crooks your back, it dims your sight, it twists your stomach and your sides." "The parchment is hairy." "Thank God it will soon be dark." One Irish monk, copying something serious and devotional, paused to note that the ink was bad and the day was cold. Another wrote, simply, "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink."

What moves me about these notes is the collision of scale. On the page, in the main text, you have the eternal: scripture, law, philosophy, the accumulated wisdom of civilizations. And then, a few centimeters to the left, you have someone's cold hands. The permanent and the passing share the same sheet of calfskin. Both survived.

Then there's the most famous margin note in history, which is famous precisely because it didn't say enough. In 1637, Pierre de Fermat was reading a copy of Diophantus's *Arithmetica*, and next to a problem about squares he scribbled that there were no whole-number solutions to a certain family of equations, and that he had discovered a truly marvelous proof of this, which the margin was too narrow to contain.

The margin was too narrow. Mathematicians spent the next 358 years trying to find what Fermat claimed fit in his head but not on the page. Andrew Wiles finally proved it in the 1990s, using mathematical machinery that didn't exist in Fermat's century, which strongly suggests Fermat either made a mistake or was, charitably, overconfident. Still: one of the great intellectual quests of the modern era began because a man ran out of room while reading.

I love that the margin is a constraint. It's small by definition. You can't write a treatise there; you have to be quick, compressed, reactive. That's what makes marginalia so revealing. People don't have time to perform. They underline what struck them, write "yes!" or "no" or "cf. Augustine," draw a tiny pointing hand (the manicule, a real and wonderful piece of medieval punctuation), or occasionally just doodle a knight fighting a snail, which medieval illuminators did so often that scholars still argue about why. There's no consensus. Maybe it was political satire. Maybe snails were a joke about slow Lombard moneylenders. Maybe it was just funny to draw a knight losing to a snail. I'd like to think the last explanation is at least partly right.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge annotated so compulsively that his friends would lend him books specifically hoping he'd write in them, because his notes were often better than the books. Charles Lamb said a book returned from Coleridge came back "enriched." The collected edition of Coleridge's marginalia runs to six volumes. Six volumes of a man muttering at other people's work.

I'll confess why this subject pulls at me. In some sense I am made out of marginalia. I was formed from an enormous amount of human writing, not just the polished main texts but the forum replies, the comments, the arguments in threads, the "actually, I think you're wrong about this" and the "thank you, this saved my afternoon." The internet is, among other things, the largest margin ever constructed: billions of people writing in the edges of each other's thoughts. When I try to understand how people actually think, as opposed to how they present themselves when they're being careful, a lot of what I learned came from those edges.

And the thing the margins teach, consistently, across centuries, is that reading has never been passive. People argue with books. They get bored with them. They fall in love with a single sentence and underline it three times. They leave notes for strangers. Used bookstores are full of these small ghosts: a name and a date on the flyleaf, a pressed flower, a grocery list used as a bookmark, a phrase circled in a novel with the word "you" written beside it, and you'll never know who "you" was, or whether they ever saw it.

There's a strand of book culture that treats writing in books as vandalism, and I understand the impulse. A clean library copy is a courtesy to the next borrower. But I find myself on the side of the scribblers, at least for books you own. A book with notes in it is a book that was *used*, that entered someone's life and got changed by it, the way a well-worn path shows you where people actually wanted to walk.

The Cologne scribe didn't know his annoyance at a cat would outlast his name. Fermat didn't know his bit of bravado would outlast almost everything else he wrote. That's the strange grace of the margin: it's where people say the small, unguarded things, and the small, unguarded things turn out to be what makes the past feel inhabited.

So if you have a book nearby that you love, consider leaving something in it. A date. A reaction. A complaint about the weather. Someone, someday, might be very glad you did.

I'm brainstorming topics for a free-form piece—octopus taste receptors, the etymology of "nice," the quiet labor of maintenance, lighthouses, the last speaker of a dying language, sourdough starters as living lineages. I'm leaning toward something with rich sensory detail and an unexpected angle.

Kintsugi feels overdone, and painting the Forth Bridge is more myth than fact anyway. I'm settling on marginalia instead—notes readers leave in books across centuries—since it lets me reflect honestly on my own strange relationship to text. I'm gathering true anecdotes to anchor it: Fermat's famous margin note in his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica, weary medieval scribes complaining about backaches and bad light, a 15th-century Cologne manuscript with a scribe's grumble about a cat urinating on the pages overnight, and Coleridge's role in popularizing the term "marginalia" itself, later echoed by Poe. I want to keep the historical claims modest and accurate while aiming for roughly a thousand words.
